p.src: Now Song Jiang led his officers and troops in a charge toward Jingnan. Each day they marched sixty li before making camp, and wherever the army passed, they did not take so much as a hair from the common people. The army reached the region of Mount Ji and encamped there. Mount Ji lay north of Jingnan and was a vital stronghold protecting it. The rebel general Li Xiang held the mountain with thirty thousand troops under his command. Li Xiang was Li Zhu's nephew, and Wang Qing had appointed him Pacification Commissioner. When he learned that Song Jiang and his men had defeated the Shannan army and captured Duan Er, he sent a messenger riding through the night to Nanfeng with an urgent report for Wang Qing and Li Zhu: “The imperial forces are formidable and have already taken two major prefectures from us. They are now coming to attack Jingnan, while another detachment under Lu Junyi has been sent to seize the Western Capital.” Li Zhu was greatly alarmed by the report and at once entered the palace to inform Wang Qing. A chamberlain carried his message inside, then returned with an order: “Tell the Military Counselor to wait. His Majesty will come out to the hall presently.” Li Zhu waited for four hours, yet there was still no sign of movement within. Li Zhu privately questioned a favored attendant with whom he was friendly, who told him, “His Majesty and Lady Duan are in the midst of a furious quarrel!” Li Zhu asked, “Why are His Majesty and the lady quarreling?” The attendant whispered in Li Zhu's ear, “His Majesty has taken a dislike to Lady Duan's looks and has not visited her apartments for a long time. That is why she is angry.” After Li Zhu had waited a while longer, a chamberlain emerged and said, “His Majesty asks whether the Military Counselor is still here.” Li Zhu replied, “I am here, awaiting his summons!” The chamberlain went in to report. Shortly afterward, Wang Qing appeared, surrounded by a throng of chamberlains and palace maids, and took his seat in the front hall. After Li Zhu had prostrated himself and completed his obeisance, he reported: “My humble subject's nephew Li Xiang sends word that Song Jiang and his men command brave generals and powerful troops, and have captured the two cities of Wanzhou and Shannan. Song Jiang has now divided his forces, sending one army to take the Western Capital and another to attack Jingnan. I humbly beg Your Majesty to dispatch troops to their relief.” When Wang Qing heard this, he flew into a rage and cried, “Song Jiang and his rabble are nothing but bandits from the marsh. How can they be so outrageously rampant?” He immediately issued a decree ordering Commander-in-Chief Du Xue to lead twelve officers and twenty thousand troops to reinforce the Western Capital; he further ordered General-in-Chief Xie Yu to lead twelve officers and twenty thousand troops to the relief of Jingnan. The two generals received their military tallies and orders, selected their troops, and put their equipment in readiness. The pretender's Privy Council assigned the officers, while the pretender's Transport Commissioner Gong Zheng conveyed provisions to supply the two generals. They took leave of Wang Qing, each led his troops along a separate route to reinforce one of the two places, and nothing more need be said of them here.

p.src: Meanwhile, Song Jiang's army reached a point ten li north of Mount Ji, where it pitched camp and prepared to attack. Scouts returned with a reliable report on the enemy's situation. After conferring with Wu Yong, Song Jiang addressed his generals: “I have heard that the men under Li Xiang are all brave and fierce warriors. Mount Ji is a vital stronghold of Jingnan. Though our forces here are twice as numerous as the rebels', they occupy the commanding terrain, while we lie beneath the mountain's northern slope, hemmed in by the enemy. That Li Xiang is cunning and treacherous. When you brothers engage him, you must watch how the situation develops and by no means treat him lightly.” He then issued an order: “Once the generals enter camp, close the gates and clear the roads. Whoever dares move about shall be executed; whoever dares speak loudly shall be executed. The army shall have no second order; whoever issues a conflicting order shall be executed. Whoever holds back an order shall be executed.” As soon as the order had been proclaimed, solemn discipline prevailed throughout the army. Song Jiang told Dai Zong to carry orders to the naval commanders Li Jun and the others, instructing them to guard the grain and transport boats with utmost care and bring the supplies forward in successive shipments to sustain the army. He sent a man with a challenge to Li Xiang, arranging for a decisive battle the following day. Vanguard Commander Song ordered Qin Ming, Dong Ping, Huyan Zhuo, Xu Ning, Zhang Qing, Qiongying, Jin Ding, and Huang Yue to lead twenty thousand troops into battle; he ordered Jiao Ting, Yu Baosi, Duan Jingzhu, and Shi Yong to lead two thousand infantrymen in felling the trees and widening the road as much as possible to make room for the battlefield. When all the assignments had been settled, Song Jiang and the remaining generals each took charge of defending the camp.

p.src: At the fifth watch next morning, the men cooked their rice and ate their fill, the horses were fed with fodder, and at daybreak the armies joined battle. Li Xiang led his subordinate generals Ma Qiang, Ma Jin, Yuan Lang, Teng Kui, and Teng Kan, with twenty thousand horse and foot, charging down upon them. These five were the bravest warriors among the rebels, and Wang Qing had appointed them Generals of the Tiger's Might. The rebel army now drew up opposite Qin Ming and the other Song forces. The rebels deployed on the level ground at the northern foot of the mountain, while many more troops stood ready above to support them. Banners fluttered within both battle lines as the two sides formed their arrays. Powerful bows and heavy crossbows secured the flanks; war drums thundered to the heavens, and colored flags dazzled the eye. When the gate banners parted in the rebel ranks, the rebel general Yuan Lang galloped forth at their head. On his head was a polished bronze helmet; over his body he wore a figured embroidered silk robe and black-lacquered, paired-inlay armor. He rode a curly-maned black steed. Red-faced and yellow-bearded, he stood nearly nine feet tall and wielded two polished tempered-steel maces, the one in his left hand weighing fifteen catties and that in his right sixteen. He shouted, “Which of you marsh bandits dares come forward and surrender his life?” In the Song ranks, Jin Ding and Huang Yue, surrendered generals from Hebei, were eager to claim the first distinction. Both spurred out of the formation together and cursed him: “A traitor rebelling against the realm is not worth mentioning!” Jin Ding brandished a great wind-cleaving saber, while Huang Yue leveled a solid-iron, steel-tipped spear, and both charged straight at Yuan Lang. Yuan Lang met them with his twin steel maces, and the three horsemen spread into a T-shaped formation and fought. After the three generals had fought for thirty bouts, Yuan Lang parried with one mace, wheeled his horse, and fled. Jin Ding and Huang Yue galloped in pursuit. Suddenly Yuan Lang turned his horse, just as Jin Ding's mount had drawn slightly ahead. As Jin Ding swung his saber down, Yuan Lang raised the mace in his left hand to meet it. With a clang, a notch was struck from the saber's edge. Before Jin Ding could recover his blade, Yuan Lang's right-hand mace smashed straight through his helmet and skull, shattering them, and knocked him from the saddle. Huang Yue's horse arrived, and his spear was already thrusting at Yuan Lang's chest. Quick-eyed and deft-handed, Yuan Lang twisted aside. Huang Yue's spear missed and passed beneath his right ribs. Yuan Lang tucked his left-hand mace beneath his arm, caught the spear shaft under his right arm in the same motion, and jerked it backward, pitching Huang Yue straight into his embrace. Yuan Lang seized him around the waist with his right arm, dragged him across onto his own horse, and hurled him to the ground. The soldiers raised a shout, rushed forward, seized him, and carried him into their lines. His horse ran straight back to its own ranks. When Qin Ming the Thunderbolt in the Song ranks saw that two generals had been lost, he flew into a rage, leaped his horse forward, raised his wolf-toothed club, and made straight for Yuan Lang. Yuan Lang brandished his maces to meet him. The two had fought for more than fifty bouts when the woman general Qiong Ying spurred forth her silver-maned horse, holding a painted halberd of the square heavens and wearing a purple-gold phoenix crown adorned with kingfisher feathers; she wore a red silk embroidered battle robe, over which was fine silver armor inlaid with gold, and rode out to aid Qin Ming. The rebel general Teng Kui saw that she was a woman, slapped his horse out of the ranks, and laughed loudly: “Song Jiang and his men truly are mere bandits! Why send a woman into battle?” Teng Kui brandished a three-pointed, double-edged saber and engaged Qiong Ying in combat. After they had fought for more than ten bouts, Qiong Ying used her halberd to sweep aside Teng Kui's saber, then wheeled her horse and fled toward her own lines. Teng Kui gave a great shout and galloped after her. From the embroidered pouch beside her saddle bow, Qiong Ying secretly took a stone. Twisting her slender waist, she took careful aim at Teng Kui and sent the stone flying. It struck him squarely in the face, splitting skin and flesh and sending blood spurting, and he tumbled from his horse. Qiong Ying suddenly turned her horse, caught up with him, and finished Teng Kui with another stroke of her painted halberd. When Teng Kan saw the woman general kill his elder brother, he flew into a rage, spurred out of the ranks, brandished a tiger-eyed, bamboo-jointed steel whip, and came at Qiong Ying.

Huyan Zhuo's only additional adornment was his other polished, eight-ridged steel whip. Before the battle lines, the two wheeled left and circled right, advancing and retreating, and fought for more than fifty bouts without either gaining the advantage. Qin Ming and Huyan Zhuo saw that the rebel generals were valiant and did not pursue them. Yuan Lang and Qin Ming each returned to his own formation, and the rebel troops withdrew up the mountain.

Together with Ling Zhen, they were to lead five thousand swift and valiant infantrymen. p.src: No sooner had the formation here been completed than the bandit commander Li Xiang of Mount Ji arrived, leading four fierce generals—Yuan Lang, Teng Kan, Ma Qiang, and Ma Jin—and twenty-five thousand troops. Teng Kan ordered a soldier to display Huang Yue's severed head on a bamboo pole and sent five thousand iron-armored cavalrymen ahead to charge the formation. Every soldier wore a deep helmet and iron armor, leaving only his eyes exposed; the horses, too, were covered in heavy armor and face guards, with only their four hooves visible beneath them. Li Xiang had seen the woman general wound one of his commanders with a flying stone the day before, so today he had equipped his men in this fashion; arrows and stones might come, but their armor would protect them. Among those five thousand cavalrymen, every two archers flanked and supported one spearman as they charged down. The troops behind them divided into two columns and closed in from both sides. Unable to withstand them, Song Jiang hurriedly retreated. Song Jiang hastily ordered the signal cannon fired. By then the enemy had shot and wounded several hundred soldiers pushing the carts. Fortunately, the war wagons held them back, preventing the armored cavalry from advancing. Though cavalry stood behind the wagons, they could not come forward to fight. At this desperate moment, a rapid succession of cannon blasts sounded behind the mountain: Lu Zhishen and his band of officers and men had scaled the heights and crossed the ridges to fight their way up the mountain. Only five thousand old and weak soldiers and one deputy commander remained in the mountain stronghold. Lu Zhishen and the others slaughtered them to the last man and seized the stockade. When Li Xiang and the others saw trouble erupt behind the mountain and hastened to withdraw, they were intercepted by Huang Xin and three other commanders on one route and Li Ying and three others on another. Song Jiang then ordered his gunners to bombard the armored cavalry, and the bandit army collapsed. Lu Zhishen, Li Kui, and the other fourteen leaders brought the infantry charging down from the mountain, scattering the bandit troops like windblown rain until they fled wildly for their lives. What a pity that so valiant a warrior as Yuan Lang was killed by cannon fire. Li Xiang, bringing up the rear, was killed by Lu Zhishen. Ma Jin and Teng Kan were slain amid the melee; only Ma Qiang escaped. Countless helmets, suits of armor, gongs, drums, and horses were captured. Of the thirty thousand troops, more than half were killed. The slopes above and below were strewn with corpses. Song Jiang recalled his troops and took a count; he too had lost more than a thousand men. As dusk had fallen, he again made camp north of Mount Ji.

Li Xiang, bringing up the rear, was killed by Lu Zhishen.
Ma Jin and Teng Kan were slain amid the melee; only Ma Qiang escaped.
Countless helmets, suits of armor, gongs, drums, and horses were captured.
Of the thirty thousand troops, more than half were killed.
The slopes above and below were strewn with corpses.
Song Jiang recalled his troops and took a count; he too had lost more than a thousand men.
As dusk had fallen, he again made camp north of Mount Ji.

p.src: The next day, Song Jiang led his officers and men up the mountain, gathered the gold, silver, and provisions, and set fire to the stockade. He richly rewarded the officers and soldiers of the three armies, recorded the merits of Lu Zhishen and the other fifteen men as well as Qiongying, and urged the army onward. After crossing Mount Ji, the great army encamped fifteen li outside Jingnan. Song Jiang conferred with the strategist Wu Yong, assigned the officers and men, and made ready to attack the city—but that need not be related here.

p.src: The tale now divides into two. The narrative returns to Lu Junyi's army, which was advancing toward the Western Capital, cutting roads through mountains and filling waterways to make crossings. Wherever they passed, bandit commanders such as Wu Shun of Baofeng and other places offered incense, flowers, lamps, and candles, surrendered their cities, and submitted to the imperial court. Lu Junyi soothed and encouraged them, then appointed Wu Shun to guard the city. The bandit commanders were moved to tears, opened their hearts without reserve, forsook evil, and returned to the right path. From then on, Lu Junyi and his men had no fear of attack from the south, and their army drove straight ahead. Within a few days they reached a place called Mount Yique, thirty li south of the Western Capital, and made camp there. Scouts learned that the city's chief commanders were the pretended Pacification Commissioner Gong Duan and Army Commander Xi Sheng, together with several fierce generals who were guarding the place. Commander Xi had studied battle formations and understood their subtleties deeply. Lu Junyi at once consulted Zhu Wu about what strategy they should use to take the city. Zhu Wu said, “I have heard that fellow Xi Sheng knows military strategy rather well. He will certainly come out to contest us. Let our army first deploy its formation. When the bandit troops arrive, we shall challenge them at our leisure.” Lu Junyi said, “Your learned counsel is perfectly clear.” He immediately dispatched the troops and arrayed them on level ground south of the mountain in the “Revolving Eight Trigrams Formation.”

p.src: As they waited, the bandit army appeared in three divisions: the center division bore red banners, the left blue banners, and the right red banners. All three arrived together. Seeing the Song army drawn up in formation, Xi Sheng ordered the blue- and red-bannered divisions to separate to the left and right and establish their camps. He climbed an observation ladder and saw that the Song troops had formed the “Revolving Eight Trigrams Formation.” Xi Sheng said, “Who would fail to recognize this formation? Just wait until I deploy a formation that will astonish them.” He ordered the troops to beat three rolls on the painted drums and erect a command platform. From atop it he waved two signal flags and arrayed the men to left and right. Once the formation was complete, he descended, mounted his horse, and ordered his foremost general to open a lane through the ranks. Then he rode before the formation to address Lu Junyi. p.src: His golden helmet flashed in the sun, streaming rosy light; his silver armor lay white as frost and swallowed the moon's reflection. His crimson battle robe was woven of splendid brocade; his yellow leather belt was studded with pearls. His green boots rested slantwise in jeweled stirrups; a gold-painted leather thong hung beside his silken whip. Before the ranks he bestrode a dragon of a horse; in his hand he held a three-foot sword gleaming like water.

u.src: His golden helmet flashed in the sun, streaming rosy light; his silver armor lay white as frost and swallowed the moon's reflection.
His crimson battle robe was woven of splendid brocade; his yellow leather belt was studded with pearls.
His green boots rested slantwise in jeweled stirrups; a gold-painted leather thong hung beside his silken whip.
Before the ranks he bestrode a dragon of a horse; in his hand he held a three-foot sword gleaming like water.

p.src: Xi Sheng reined his horse and rode straight before the formation, shouting, “Whom do you hope to deceive with your ‘Revolving Eight Trigrams Formation’? But can you recognize my formation?” Hearing that Xi Sheng wished to compete in battle formations, Lu Junyi climbed the observation ladder with Zhu Wu to survey the field. In the bandit formation, three men made a squad, three squads formed a company, and five companies made a battalion. It was square without and round within, great formations enclosing small ones, all joined and linked together. Zhu Wu said to Lu Junyi, “This is Li Yaoshi's ‘Six-Flower Formation.’ Yaoshi took Marquis Wu's Eight Formations and adapted them into the Six-Flower Formation. The bandit commander thinks no one on our side can recognize his formation; he does not know that we need only transform our Eight Trigrams Formation into eight times eight, making sixty-four divisions—the very method of Marquis Wu's Diagram of the Eight Formations—and we can break his Six-Flower Formation.” Lu Junyi rode before the formation and shouted, “What is so remarkable about your paltry ‘Six-Flower Formation’?” Xi Sheng said, “Do you dare attack it?” Lu Junyi laughed aloud. “What difficulty could there be in such a trifling formation?” Lu Junyi returned to the formation. From the command platform, Zhu Wu swept his signal flags left and right, transforming their ranks into the Diagram of the Eight Formations. Zhu Wu had Lu Junyi transmit an order that Yang Zhi, Sun An, and Bian Xiang were to lead one thousand armored cavalrymen in an assault on the formation. “Today belongs to the element metal. Drive all the troops from our formation's king position at Li in the south forward in a single charge.” Yang Zhi and the others obeyed and sounded three rolls of the drums. The commanders advanced, swept aside the bandit army's western gate banners, and fought their way inside. Meanwhile, Lu Junyi led Ma Ling and the other officers and soldiers in a covering assault, and the bandit army suffered a crushing defeat.

p.src: Now Yang Zhi and the others, having fought their way into the army, came directly upon Xi Sheng, who was fleeing north under the protection of several fierce generals. Eager to win distinction, Sun An and Bian Xiang led their men in pursuit, unaware that they were penetrating deep into dangerous ground. Suddenly, a gong sounded behind the hillside, and a formidable body of troops charged out. Yang Zhi, Sun An, and the others tried to retreat, but it was already too late. Indeed:
